The joint Scattered Spider advisory, revised July 29, 2025, describes attackers gathering password-reset information through calls, then persuading IT help-desk staff to reset passwords and/or transfer MFA tokens. That enabled account takeovers in single sign-on environments.

The distinction matters: convincing someone to reset access is different from defeating the technology protecting it. The same advisory recommends phishing-resistant MFA, including FIDO/WebAuthn or PKI-based implementations.

I’d include one question in an MFA review: when someone cannot provide their usual proof, what independent evidence must the help desk verify before authorizing a password reset or MFA-token transfer?

That’s a decision about who gets trusted as the account owner. request.task: You are a strict LinkedIn publish-quality evaluator. Score the finished post, not the raw topic, from 0 (absent) to 5 (exceptional) on each named dimension. Judge whether the post is understandable, useful, specific, distinctive, interesting, shareable, and authentic enough to publish. Do not reward clickbait, engagement bait, unsupported specificity, or generic LinkedIn polish. Use the supplied evidence only to judge whether concrete details are grounded. This is a publish-readiness heuristic, not a promise of virality. These ratings are not calibrated to the author's human judgments or engagement outcomes. Apply the rating anchors to each dimension; never inflate scores to meet a threshold. Use the same brief and voice context as the writer. Identify the largest fixable defect first; missing factual support is an evidence-brief gap, not permission to invent a better story. Return JSON only.
